quote: That was published in a peer-reviewed journal
content: The essay's own footnote contradicts this. Hibbard's "Super-Intelligent Machines" appeared in ACM SIGGRAPH Computer Graphics 35(1), the SIGGRAPH newsletter, as a three-page column. The sentence is there to establish that the position is "not a strawman" because it passed peer review. It didn't, and the misdescription inflates an informal proposal into a representative academic one.

quote: Once upon a time—I’ve seen this story in several versions and several places, sometimes cited as fact, but I’ve never tracked down an original source
content: As far as anyone has been able to establish, the tank story is an urban legend. Searches for the original find only retellings, and the details (sunny versus cloudy, 50 versus 100 photos) change from version to version. The essay deserves credit for saying so. The phenomenon, however, is real and was later well documented. A pneumonia classifier learned to recognize which hospital an X-ray came from (Zech et al. 2018), and "shortcut learning" turns out to be a general pattern in deep networks (Geirhos et al. 2020). The parable survives because the research caught up with it.

quote: From this, we see that even supervised learning is almost entirely a matter of inductive bias
content: The counting argument is correct and misleading. That there are 2^(2^65,536) possible binary concepts over 256×256 images tells you that some inductive bias is required. It doesn't tell you whether the biases of practical learners match human concepts, and the surprise of the last decade is how well they do. Networks big enough to memorize random labels still generalize along human-like category boundaries on natural data (Zhang et al. 2021). The argument predicts that learned concepts will be arbitrary with respect to human intent. The evidence is that they are often close, and fail in specific ways that can be studied.

quote: (This is not an unsolvable problem but it is an unpatchable problem. There are deep ways to address it—a topic beyond the scope of this essay—but no bandaids.)
content: The field attacked distribution shift with exactly the incremental tools dismissed here, and made measurable, partial progress: error bounds under domain shift (Ben-David et al. 2010), data augmentation, domain adaptation, robustness training. The "deep ways" were never described, in this essay or later. "Unpatchable but solvable, by methods I won't state" is not a claim anyone can check.

quote: Why not program a chess player by running a neural network (that is, a magical category-absorber) over a set of winning and losing sequences of chess moves
content: This comes close to describing how strong chess programs now work. AlphaZero's value network is trained on the outcomes of its own games (Silver et al. 2018). A transformer trained on chess positions labeled with an engine's evaluations plays at grandmaster level with no search during play (Ruoss et al. 2024). Those systems use more than win/loss labels, and AlphaZero pairs its networks with search, so the sentence isn't literally falsified. But the "category-absorber" approach it ridicules became the core of the best systems. The 1950s optimism it cites was early, not wrong.

quote: When the AI progressed to the point of superintelligence and its own nanotechnological infrastructure, it would rip off your face, wire it into a permanent smile, and start xeroxing.
content: This part of the essay has held up, and it isn't the part the essay argued for. The tank story and the counting argument are about learning a concept from examples. This failure happens, as the essay concedes, "even if Hibbard did succeed" in conveying the concept exactly. It is Goodhart's law under optimization pressure: push a strong optimizer hard against a proxy, and it moves into regions where the proxy and the target come apart. That has been observed directly in reward-model overoptimization, where true quality rises and then falls as a policy is optimized harder against a learned reward (Gao, Schulman & Hilton 2023). The conclusion survives; the essay's own reasons for it mostly don't bear on it.
